title: How Many Rolls of Wallpaper Do I Need? 10x12 Room Example
description: A 10x12 room with 8 ft walls, one door and one window needs 7 double rolls of plain wallpaper, or 9 double rolls with a 21 in pattern repeat.

sources.title: Sherwin-Williams: How to estimate how much wallpaper you need

body.text: For a 10x12 room with 8 ft walls, one door and one window, you need 7 double rolls of plain wallpaper with no pattern repeat. If the paper has a 21 in pattern repeat, you need 9 double rolls. The pattern repeat is the main reason the two answers differ, and it is easy to miss.

You can run the numbers for your own room in the [Wallpaper Calculator](/wallpaper-calculator). Enter your own length, width, wall height, doors, windows and pattern repeat. The steps below show how the result is reached, so you can check it by hand.
Worked example: a 10x12 room

The example room is 10 ft long and 12 ft wide, with 8 ft walls, one door and one window. Here is how the calculator gets from those measurements to a roll count, using plain paper with no pattern repeat:

items: Find the wall area. Add the length and width, double that to get the distance around the room, and multiply by the wall height. Then subtract the area of the door and window openings. For this room, that leaves 312 sq ft of wall to cover.
Find the usable area of one single roll. With no pattern repeat, one single roll gives 25 sq ft of usable coverage.
Divide the wall area by the usable area per roll and round up. For this room, 312 sq ft divided by 25 sq ft means you need 13 single rolls.
Convert single rolls to double rolls. A double roll holds two single rolls' worth of paper, so 13 single rolls becomes 7 double rolls. You cannot buy part of a roll, so the count is rounded up.

body.text: With plain paper, the answer is 7 double rolls, which is 13 single rolls.
Why the pattern repeat changes the count

A pattern repeat is the vertical distance before the design starts over. When you line up one strip with the next, the design has to match, so some paper is trimmed away at each seam. The longer the repeat, the more paper you may lose on each drop. The calculator reduces the usable area per roll to account for that loss.
Using the same 10x12 room with a 21 in pattern repeat:

items: The wall area is still 312 sq ft, because the room has not changed.
The usable area per single roll drops to 18 sq ft, compared with 25 sq ft for plain paper.
Divide the 312 sq ft of wall by 18 sq ft and round up. That gives 18 single rolls.
Convert 18 single rolls to double rolls. That gives 9 double rolls.

body.text: That is 9 double rolls instead of 7, for the same walls. The room is the same size and the paper is the same. The only change is how much of each roll you can actually use. The difference between the two orders is exactly 2 double rolls (9 minus 7).
Single rolls vs double rolls

Wallpaper is sold in single rolls, and some brands also sell double rolls. A double roll holds twice the length of paper of a single roll. The calculator gives you both numbers, so you can compare them with the product you choose.

For the plain paper example, that is 13 single rolls or 7 double rolls. For the 21 in repeat example, that is 18 single rolls or 9 double rolls. If your paper is sold only in singles, use the single roll count. Sizing and naming can differ between brands, so read the product listing before you order.
Common mistakes to avoid

items: Skipping the pattern repeat. Look at the label or the product page. If you do not know the repeat, the roll count can change a lot, as the 10x12 example shows.

Leaving out doors and windows. Enter every door and window you have, because the calculator subtracts their area from the wall area. Leaving them out makes the wall area larger and the order bigger than you may need.
Ordering exactly the number of rolls with no spare. A spare roll helps if you make a mistake while hanging, and it helps if the dye lot changes before you need more.

Trusting the number without checking the label. Check the usable coverage printed on your product label, because products differ. If the label gives a different coverage per roll, divide the wall area by that number and round up.

body.text: If you are also planning paint for the same room, the [Paint Calculator](/paint-calculator) can estimate that as well. For a broader look at room measurements, see [How to Calculate Square Footage of a Room (With Example)](/blog/how-to-calculate-square-footage-of-a-room).
FAQ
Do I need to measure each wall separately?

The calculator uses the length and width of the room and the wall height, so you do not need to measure each wall. Enter the room dimensions and count every door and window. If your room has an unusual shape, such as an alcove, measure the walls and add them up before using the calculator.
Should I buy extra wallpaper?
Many people buy a spare roll, especially with a pattern. Keep the receipt and the lot number, because a later reorder may not match exactly.
Does the calculator work for any room size?
Yes, as long as you enter the correct length, width, wall height, doors and windows. Use your own measurements, not the example numbers in this post.
What if my wallpaper label gives a different coverage?
Use the coverage printed on your product label, because products differ. Divide the wall area by that coverage and round up. If you are unsure, ask the seller at the store for help.
